why each step is the way it is
The two messages differ on purpose: "N required" for a fixed-arity
function, "at least N required" for a variadic one.
Representation, not policy — so it is unconditional and
allow_dynamic_type. go-cty has no wrapper around a dynamic-typed value, so the
wrapper has to come off before any type check, or the check asks a different
question from go-cty's. Each removed wrapper's marks move onto what it wrapped:
in go-cty those marks would already be on the value, so dropping them here would
declassify a value merely for arriving through a dynamic slot.
The marks are discarded here because the call collects them separately in
step 4, and a Type callback that consulted marks would make the return type
allow_unknown is not consulted in step 2
at all. A return type has to be computable from unknown values, which is
the whole point of computing it separately from the answer.
go-cty returns the moment it meets an inexactly typed argument.
The later arguments are never checked at all
, so a null or a mistyped value
a DynamicVal is not an error — the call is already decided to be
DynamicVal. Checking them anyway failed 20 of the 83 stdlib functions on
f(DynamicVal, null), a call Terraform accepts.

: that is the function answering. Anything else becomes

go-cty panics here rather than returning an error: a result that does not
match the type its own Type callback promised is a bug in the function, not in
the call, and callers are entitled not to handle it.
There is no type yet for a refinement to be about, and the gate is on the
, not the arguments: jsondecode of an unknown string returns an unknown
from perfectly concrete arguments, and refining it anyway was measured
as a divergence against regex, concat, merge and csvdecode.
Refinement runs on the known path too. Refining a known value is a claim the
